title: Reading scales
examples: How do I know what the lines mean?
Can I use this scale for liquid?
What is the biggest number I can read?

explain.say: A scale has marks and numbers. You read it to find how much. A ruler is a scale for length.
Put one end of the object at zero. Look where the other end stops. Read that number.
Some scales have small lines between the numbers. Count the small steps from one number to the next.
From zero to ten there are five small steps. So each step is worth two.
A measuring jug shows how much water it holds. Bend down so your eyes are level with the water. Then read the line.

draw.text: Read the jug at eye level

faq.q: What do the numbers on the ruler mean?
faq.a: The numbers show the length in units like centimetres. You read the number that lines up with the end of the object.
asks: What do the numbers on the ruler mean?

faq.q: Do I always start at zero when measuring?
faq.a: Yes, put one end of the object at the zero mark. If you start somewhere else, count the steps from where you started.
asks: Do I always start at zero when measuring?
Does it matter where I start?

faq.q: How do I read a measuring jug for water?
faq.a: Put the jug on a flat table. Bend down so your eyes are level with the water. The line that matches the water tells you the amount.
asks: How do I read a measuring jug for water?

faq.q: What are the small lines on the scale?
faq.a: The small lines show smaller steps between the numbers. They help you measure more exactly.
asks: What are the small lines on the scale?
What do the tiny lines mean?

faq.q: Can I use a ruler for liquids?
faq.a: No, use a measuring jug for liquids. A ruler measures length, and a jug measures how much liquid there is.
asks: Can I use a ruler for liquids?
Is this ruler good for juice?

facts: Rulers measure straight length in units like centimetres.
Measuring jugs are used to measure liquids like water or juice.
Always read liquid levels at eye level for accuracy.
Measurements must always start counting from the zero mark.

quiz.say: Look at the ruler. Tap how long the pencil is.
quiz.why: Count the centimetres from 2 to 7. That is 5 centimetres.

wrong.0: The pencil ends at 7, but it starts at 2 instead of 0.
wrong.2: The 9 comes from adding 2 and 7, but you count the gap between them.

quiz.say: Tap where your eyes go to read a measuring jug.
quiz.why: When your eyes are level with the water, you see the true line.

wrong.0: From above, the water line can look like it is at a different mark.
wrong.2: From below, the water line can look like it is at a different mark.

quiz.say: Look at the scale. Tap what one small step is worth.
quiz.why: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 5 steps to reach 10.

wrong.0: Steps of 1 would need 10 steps to reach 10.
wrong.1: Steps of 5 would reach 10 in just 2 steps.
